articles.headline: "We didn't want the brooding hero out for revenge": How quiet lulls and a bird-sketching lead make Control Resonant a more introspective kind of action game
keyFacts: Control Resonant differs from the original game by featuring quieter, pensive moments between intense combat encounters.
Director Mikael Kasurinen stated that they wanted Dylan to be a gentle, introspective hero who does not default to violence.
Kasurinen declined to discuss future plans for the franchise, noting it is too early to talk about the future.
body: Like the repeating pattern effect afflicting its warped Manhattan, Control Resonant threw me for a loop. One minute I would be brutally slashing and smashing my way through hordes of inhuman enemies, enacting a never-ending chain combo of bellowing violence with my Aberrant, and the next minute I would be scanning nearby rooftops for signs of a squeaking purple dragon plushie to give to a very wiggly dog (who, I was pretty sure, could teleport). Combat often felt desperate and bloody; knockdown-and-drag-out brawls that had me limping away like John Wick after a particularly messy gunkata affair. Still, these fights all ended eventually, and in their place was not always more action-RPG battling but, more often, an odd sense of melancholic peace and quiet. It’s a strange dichotomy I’ve been thinking about nearly nonstop since I finished my first playthrough.
Spoilers/Revelations for Control Resonant ahead. Don’t say we didn’t warn/notify you.

Control Resonant is, as has been extensivly documented and commented upon, a very different game to the original Control. But beyond the most obvious action differences (Jesse packs heat while Dylan speaks softly, carrying a big stick), Resonant seems much more inclined towards these quieter moments. For one thing, the lack of enemy mob respawns, outside of specific major plot beats and world-resetting boss victories, gave me the time to breathe and take in my surroundings in a way Control never let me do. The Oldest House was disorienting by design, and it used the constant Hiss pressure to keep me motivated, always moving towards the next objective or plot point. Control Resonant, conversely, allows the mind to wander.

This makes sense when you look at who you're playing as. A more introspective adventure is the perfect speed for Dylan, someone trained from childhood to be capable of superhuman violence, and is now equipped with the perfect, shapeshifting tool for the job - yet spends one of his first scenes in Resonant enjoying the fresh, crisp Autumn stink of New York City for the first time in his life. When he stumbles out of the Oldest House right at the beginning of the game, the camera shifting focus to a single leaf, floating on the wind to greet him a la Forrest Gump while the dreamy strings and flutes of Petri Alanko’s soundtrack play wistfully behind it, we don't see a killer unleashed. We see a prisoner liberated, and are invited to feel with him the elation that came with finally being truly free. Even if it's coupled with the sadness and conflict of knowing, with his sister missing and Manhattan in danger, he can't simply disappear into the ether.

"We agreed on his direction early," Control Resonant director Mikael Kasurinen tells me. "We didn’t want the brooding hero out for revenge. We wanted someone who doesn’t reach for violence as the first solution, someone who can see beauty where others see horror. He feels empathy for the monsters because he sees himself in them."

Even though much of Control let us in on Jesse’s running inner monologue, I wouldn’t classify it as a very introspective narrative, because Jesse isn’t a very introspective person. She’s motivated by action, living in the moment, constantly moving forward, and this is reflected in the way her and her brother’s story is told in that first game. Jesse would come across a document, a recording, some evidence of the FBC’s abusive treatment of Dylan, and she would feel genuinely terrible about this - but only momentarily, her innate sense of urgency almost forcing her to put her thoughts on hold until the latest threat is dealt with. And even when she does react, she's rarely truly surprised, having known for ages that these were the shadowy G-men who stole Dylan away; any new information mainly just reinforces her existing motivation to find and rescue him.

By contrast, Control Resonant is almost primarily about Dylan’s interiority: his guilt, his need to atone, and ultimately, who he is outside of the clutches of both the FBC and the Hiss. This also reflects on the exterior, in the way the game ebbs and flows between cavalcades of carnage and the many quiet, pensive moments throughout.

"The contradiction is that he has no doubts about himself as a parautilitarian," Kasurinen says. "He knows he can face the paranatural threats and win. What he doubts is whether he deserves to exist as a person. He also has a gentle heart. He wants to help, and he has no trouble saying what he sees and feels."

A perfect example of this type of moment happens in the Sinkhole, a particularly intense, Earth-piercing concentration of the citywide Patterning. The trip to the bottom, using an ad-hoc "diving bell" of cobbled-together FBC sensors, comprises multiple levels of tricky fight scenes, as dozens of crimson fiends coagulate around you in increasingly abstract-looking patterned apartment blocks. The Hiss are brutal here, and you have to work quickly to dispatch each new wave or risk getting overwhelmed. Upon finally reaching the bottom, you’re faced with one more crushing attack, including one massive, flying monstrosity you've likely never faced before. The fight is hard, and tense, but eventually you prevail - only for your diving bell to be yanked back up to the surface, leaving you behind. A diver trapped at the bottom of a paranatural Marianas Trench.

Control Resonant never tells you outright how to escape the subsequent maze; it just lets you navigate the strange geometry and variable gravity on your own, leaving you alone - despite the attempts of handler Zoe to raise you on the radio - with your thoughts. Music rings out, and it’s unclear whether it’s something Zoe is playing for you or if it’s happening in your head, especially as crackling snippets of comms chatter reveal that your minutes stuck in the Sinkhole have lasted hours on the surface.

It's a powerful sequence, heightening the struggle of escape with the dread of hearing how the world is going by outside. And it works because, even with the music, it's quiet enough for you to focus on those feelings. It's a big moment for Dylan as a character, too. He's spent most of his life helpless, first as a 'guest' of the FBC, then as a brainwashed agent of the Hiss. Threatened with entombment in a reality-breaking pit, his voice wobbles with fear, yet he chooses - for one of the first times in decades - to reject that helplessness and save himself. He weighs up those doubts, and decides he deserves to exist.

I still have thoughts on Control Resonant that I haven't reconciled, especially around Jesse. The first female main protagonist of a Remedy game, she does end up sidelined in favor of exploring the inner workings of her brother, including through a series of quests where she risks being literally erased by the Patterning. Then there's the ending that (seriously, spoiler re-warning) has her pull a kind of messed-up UNO reverse card on Dylan's ultimate sacrifice, ensuring that he lives while she... ends up where Dylan had been, all the way back at the beginning of the game. What do we do with this?

"It’s too early to talk about the future," Kasurinen replies when I ask if we might get a new glimpse of the Fadens soon; perhaps a peek at a 'Control: Gestalt,' if you will. Thoughh... yeah, for sure, of course. "But thematically I wanted the two games to complement each other and show two different sides of the same world. The world stays the same, but we see it through a new protagonist."

As someone who played through Control quite thoroughly a few years ago, I didn’t initially feel like I needed a whole lot of extra information about the myriad ways Casper Darling was a wretched manipulator who’d abused Dylan. But on the other side of this, I was occasionally quite taken by the lengths Control Resonant went to give Dylan chances to heal on-screen, whether it was by befriending a dog, hearing new music for the first time since childhood (courtesy of music fan and radio misappropriator Zoe), or drawing perfect still-life tableaus out of piles of garbage he found, ruminating on the idyllic scenes he imagined as he sketched and thinking about how he’d like to experience them once the Altered World Event was over. One drawing, which was just a self-portrait of Dylan in his 40s, sitting on a bench surrounded by birds, hit me profoundly. There is something powerful about imagining a peaceful future for yourself when all evidence has always pointed to the contrary, and there's no better time to have those thoughts than in a moment of quiet.

articles.headline: Fanfic Hub Archive of Our Own Faces Weeks Offline
keyFacts: The fan-fiction site Archive of Our Own faces an unplanned shutdown expected to last between two and four weeks, according to the site.
The platform is operated by the Organization for Transformative Works, which stated that service might return sooner in a degraded state.
Millions of users are currently locked out of the site following a series of intermittent disruptions throughout October.
body: October has been a rocky month for readers of the fan-run fiction site Archive of Our Own. Now, a routine disruption has escalated into a crisis. What began as an estimated 12-hour unplanned outage has ballooned into a multi-week shutdown, leaving millions of users locked out of the site following a series of intermittent disruptions throughout the month.
The platform is operated by the Organization for Transformative Works.

“We estimate that service restoration for #AO3 will take around 2 weeks, but it could be up to 4 weeks,” the site said in an update posted Thursday to its status page, and disseminated via Bluesky and Tumblr. “We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved.”
More from CNET
That update followed an initial notification, 12 hours earlier, with the estimate “AO3 maintenance is in progress. We expect it to take at least 12 hours, but it may take longer.”
An Archive of Our Own representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
While it’s possible the outage is related to the web-wide PHP patch emergency from earlier this month, the Organization for Transformative Works patched its sister site, Fanlore, on Oct. 21.

So it seems like patching the humongous AO3 repository would come with ample warning, especially from a volunteer team with a reputation for solid communication. Instead, an outage of this magnitude hit readers out of nowhere, landing with all the subtlety of a Looney Tunes anvil.
If you need a stopgap alternative to feed your fanfic need, you can try Wattpad or FanFiction.

articles.headline: Zverev seals world number one spot after win
keyFacts: Alexander Zverev will replace Jannik Sinner as the men's world number one on Monday after defeating Tallon Griekspoor at the Erste Bank Open.
Zverev secured the ranking after winning two Grand Slam titles this year while rivals Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz missed time due to injury.
Zverev will next face British number one Arthur Fery in the quarter-finals in Vienna.
body: - Published
Alexander Zverev will replace Jannik Sinner as the menâs world number one at his earliest opportunity after reaching the quarter-finals in Vienna.

Germanyâs Zverev was already guaranteed to finish 2026 as the ATPâs leading player, but made sure he will rise to the summit on Monday with a 6-4 7-5 win over Tallon Griekspoor at the Erste Bank Open.
Zverev, 29, is the second German to reach the pinnacle of the men's tour after Boris Becker in 1991.
The achievement is a testament to his body of work this year, having won two Grand Slam titles and 64 of his 80 matches.
"It's been a wait but sometimes you have to wait for the best things in life," said Zverev, who is the second oldest man to top the rankings for the first time.
"I'm super happy, super thrilled - I have no words for this year."
At the start of the year it seemed unthinkable that anybody other than Sinner or Carlos Alcaraz would become world number one.

But the dominant duo have missed large chunks of this season through injury, opening the door for Zverev - who won the French Open and US Open titles with at least one of the pair absent - to take over.
Going into 2026, Alcaraz led the rankings with 12,050 points, closely followed by Sinner on 11,500.
The pair's duopoly - splitting all of the eight Grand Slam titles in 2024 and 2025 between them - was illustrated by the huge gap to the rest of the field.
Third-ranked Zverev had 5,110 points - closer numerically to the 2,221st player in the world than the top two.
Both his major triumphs came without having to face Sinner or Alcaraz, and he did not face a top-10 player until beating Ben Shelton in the New York final.
As the season entered its final stretch, Zverev achieved what many thought was impossible by securing the year-end number one ranking when Alcaraz lost in Shanghai on 12 October.

Zverev knew he still could not overtake Sinner until 2 November at the earliest, but beat Griekspoor to become the first man other than Sinner and Alcaraz to top the rankings since Novak Djokovic in June 2024.
Zverev conceded he would "maybe not" be the world's best player if both his rivals were "healthy and at the top of their game".

But he has efficiently beaten what has been in front of him, recording the greatest season of a career which had threatened to fall short of the lofty expectations placed on him since emerging as a teenage prodigy.
Fery continues to prove himself - and faces Zverev next
Zverev goes on to face British number one Arthur Fery in the quarter-finals - a repeat of their Wimbledon semi-final.
Fery, 24, made an unexpected run to the SW19 last four in July, but continued to prove he belongs among the world's best with a 6-4 5-7 6-4 win over Italy's Lorenzo Musetti in Vienna.
Trailing 4-2 in the decider, Fery showed his mental fortitude by breaking straight back and then overcoming what seemed to be cramp to serve out an impressive victory.
It is easy to forget Fery is still inexperienced at the elite level following his Wimbledon heroics.

Beating former world number five Musetti - now ranked 26th after injury - represents his biggest win by ranking on the regular ATP Tour and provides another opportunity to test himself against the very best.
However, Cameron Norrie fell short of his best victory of the season when world number five Daniil Medvedev saved match point to win their last-16 match.
A frustrating year has seen Norrie drop to 41st in the world rankings and exit each of the past three Grand Slam tournaments in the first round.
But the 31-year-old showed his key attributes - tenacity, athleticism and controlled aggression - to threaten a huge upset against Medvedev.
Third seed Medvedev, fresh from winning the Almaty title last week, was left angrily punching the surface when he fell a break down in the deciding set.
Norrie served for the match at 5-3 40-30, but Medvedev picked off his opponent's serve-volley attempt and fought back to win 4-6 6-3 7-6 (7-1).
Elsewhere, second seed Alcaraz progressed with a 6-1 7-6 (13-11) win over Georgia's Nikoloz Basilashvili.

articles.headline: Jude Bellingham’s dad receives special England call-up
keyFacts: Mark Bellingham has received his first call-up to represent the England Veterans Over 50s squad.
The 50-year-old former non-league striker will play in an international match against the Republic of Ireland this weekend.
He joins his sons Jude and Jobe in representing England on the international football stage.
body: Jude Bellingham’s dad, Mark, has been called up to represent England Veterans Over 50s against the Republic of Ireland.
Having turned 50 in March of this year, Bellingham Sr. is going to pick up an international cap playing for his country.
Bellingham’s dad, Mark, has been called up to the England Veterans Over 50s squad for a clash against the Republic of Ireland this weekend Getty
He is a former striker who had a 17-year career in non-league, playing for 22 different teams throughout his playing days.
Mark made his most appearances for Leamington between 2008 and 2009 and Bromsgrove Sporting in 2014, also playing for Cheltenham Town and Newport County in the late 90s.
Mark retired from football in 2019 but continued to play in veterans tournaments, leading to his call-up.
Bellingham’s dad called up for England
England Veterans Over 50s have announced their squad for a match against the Republic of Ireland this weekend.
And Mark has been included in the 18-player line-up.
There will also be an Over 60s side playing Ireland on the same day.
They team wrote: “England Veterans have announced their squads for a double helping of international football against the Republic of Ireland on Sunday 1st November in Cambridgeshire.
“The Over 50’s kick off at 2:15pm and the Over 60’s at 4:15pm at the Elite Football Complex, Cambridgeshire.”
It is Mark’s first call-up to represent his country.
He has followed in his son’s footsteps, with Jude the Three Lions’ leading star and Jobe Bellingham playing for the Under-21s.
Bellingham has been a superstar for England, with his younger brother Jobe playing for the U21s and his dad now playing for the Veterans Over 50s AFP
Three Bellinghams on the international stage
Bellingham Sr. will hope for a dream start to life as an international player to keep up with his two sons.
Jude, of course, is a superstar for England , already picking up 60 caps for his country at just 23 years old.
He scored seven goals at the 2026 World Cup for the Three Lions this summer, leading the nation alongside newly-crowned Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane .
In total, he has 14 goals and 15 assists in 60 games for England.
As for Jobe, he is one of the leaders in the U21s camp, captaining the Young Lions in his last 11 appearances.
Altogether he has 12 caps for the team, scoring once and assisting four goals.

articles.headline: Report claims AI is recommending risky security moves — so maybe you shouldn't hand over full control of your systems just yet
keyFacts: A study by Illumio reported that 70% of organizations delegate critical security decisions to AI that humans made a year ago.
The research found that 76% of organizations experienced security issues due to AI over the past year.
Raghu Nandakumara of Illumio stated that businesses must set strict limits on AI access and actions to contain unexpected behavior.
body: - Report says AI is being given too much authority and autonomy to handle business-critical security decisions
- 70% of organizations delegate decisions to AI that would have been made by a human 12 months ago
- A “control gap” exists between the authority given to AI and an organization’s ability to audit it

Delegating complicated decisions to AI is leading organizations to place relatively new technology in charge of user permissions, in control of sensitive data, and risk security issues, new research has claimed.
A study by Illumio looked into how organizations are handing decision recently performed by humans to AI, without apparently taking into account the potential for serious issues to arise.
It found the majority (70%) of organizations are delegating previously human-made decisions to AI, but only around half (49%) can see what action is taken by an AI agent an audit it.
AI recommendations

The nature of AI agents makes this a particularly risky strategy, and the research has found that an incredible 56% of organizations are willing to accept greater cyber risks than 12 months ago. Almost half of that group (47%) have admitted to permitting AI actions in production environments.

Allowing AI agents to have free run of enterprise data, applications, and infrastructure is leading to wholly avoidable situations. Illumio’s research found that a control gap between the rules that organizations believe AI agents are operating within and what the technology is actually capable of.

Some 76% of organizations have experienced one or more security issues thanks to AI in the past year, with 35% revealing that following AI recommendations would result in a security risk. Meanwhile, 26% reported AI agents or tools had connected to other systems without the necessary approval.
More worrying is the 24% of organizations reporting AI’s drive to access data it shouldn’t be able to see, and another 24% stating it has triggered (or produced) an unauthorized action.

Strict limits

Of course, AI is already used within cybersecurity, and has proved successful with multiple vendors rolling out AI-enhanced solutions. But while 67% of organizations are using AI cybersecurity tools, 32% let AI conduct investigations without human oversight and 29% permit the software to deploy code changes completely unsupervised.
“The biggest AI risk may not be a system that breaks its rules. It may be one that was never given meaningful limits in the first place," noted Raghu Nandakumara, VP of Industry Strategy at Illumio.
Unleashing AI agents without constraints has left businesses struggling to control the software.

As Nandakumara observes, AI agents are persistent, and attempting to outwit their next move is pointless. Instead, “businesses must set strict limits on what they can access and do, then enforce those limits within the application and across the underlying infrastructure. That is how you contain unexpected behavior before it causes real damage.”

articles.headline: Windows 11 gets right-click menu improvements as PC revenue slides
keyFacts: Microsoft is rolling out a Windows 11 preview update that adds a customize menu button for the right-click menu.
The update follows Microsoft reporting a continued decline in the business of selling Windows licenses for new PCs.
The preview update also introduces Cloud Rebuild, a recovery option that reinstalls Windows 11 directly from the cloud.
body: Microsoft is beginning the rollout of a Windows 11 preview update that finally addresses a persistent power user complaint with the operating system: the right-click menu that obliterated years of muscle memory on command locations, and hid others behind an additional click. The timing for the release is notable, as the announcement comes alongside Microsoft's quarterly financial report that saw a continued decline in the business of selling Windows licenses for new PCs.

The preview update, KB5127936 , is cumulative for Windows 11 versions 26H2 and 25H2. The update will be a gradual rollout before eventually moving on to a normal rollout for all Windows 11 devices once it reaches general availability. The highlight of the new update should calm annoyed users who have spent years with custom scripts and services in an attempt to shape Windows the way they'd prefer it. Users will get a "customize menu" button that controls what commands appear when they right-click their mouse. Users can toggle built-in commands such as Send To or Create Shortcut on or off, rearrange what appears on the main menu, and control which third-party extensions show up in either the main or submenus. The gripe with the right-click menu had been that Microsoft hid familiar command locations behind a top row of icons while moving other familiar commands under the "Show more options" submenu. Now, Windows users will have the ability to customize the whole thing around their habits.
The original Windows 11 right-click menu is a mess.
Credit:
Microsoft

The new preview also highlights a new Windows feature called Cloud Rebuild, a recovery option that can reinstall Windows 11 directly from the cloud, even when an existing Windows 11 fails to boot. Cloud Rebuild will pull the Windows 11 image and needed system drivers directly from Windows Update. Users will not need a custom recovery image or external media to reinstall Windows. There is an important distinction to note however. Microsoft classified Cloud Rebuild as a recovery option, but it behaves more like a fresh Windows install than a repair, as existing applications and files will not be included. Those worried about data security have the option to sanitize entire system drives prior to reinstalling. For a full list of improvements coming to Windows 11, including changes to Xbox mode and settings, you can view the official Microsoft release announcement .

body: Patrick Stewart, best known for his roles in Star Trek and X-Men, has died at age 86. A message posted to Stewart’s Instagram account says the actor died in his Los Angeles home on Wednesday “following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.”
Patrick Stewart has died at age 86
Stewart was best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek.

Born in 1940 in Mirfield, Yorkshire, England, Stewart began his acting career in theater. He eventually landed the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation, which ran from 1987 to 1994. Stewart returned as the Star Trek captain in subsequent films, including Star Trek: Generations (1994), Star Trek: First Contact (1996), Star Trek: Insurrection (1998), and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002). “His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre,” the message on Instagram says. “He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise.”

articles.headline: What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery
keyFacts: Researchers found that over 500 Antarctic penguins initially suspected of dying from bird flu were actually killed by avian cholera, a bacterial disease.
Wildlife veterinarian Ralph Vanstreels said the findings demonstrate that diseases other than bird flu are spreading among Antarctic bird populations.
Researchers said international collaboration is necessary to effectively track traveling pathogens that do not respect borders.
body: What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery
Sailing toward the Danger Islands, Dr. Ralph Vanstreels had a good idea of what he might find: A lot of dead Adélie penguins.
It was March 2024 and a virus had been sweeping through the area, leaving deceased birds in its wake.
Vanstreels got the crime right but the culprit wrong. There were dead penguins but a virus was not to blame.
As his vessel pulled up to a landing ramp on one of the islands — located just off the Antarctic Peninsula — Vanstreels and his fellow researchers immediately noticed bumps in the snow.

"Was each bump a rock or was it a carcass? We had to do quite a bit of intensive searching [through the snow]," says Vanstreels, who is based in Argentina and is a wildlife veterinarian with the University of California, Davis.
The team ultimately found more than 537 penguin carcasses on just the ramp, which he estimates was about the size of an airport runway.

There were many more carcasses elsewhere on the Danger Islands, which are home to two mega colonies for penguins. The researchers estimate there were thousands of dead Adélie penguins and other species of birds. But they had to work quickly and couldn't do a complete count, Vanstreels says.
"You cannot stay there very long because you might be locked down with an iceberg blocking your way out," he says.
As the team has pieced together this tragic penguin mystery, Vanstreels says, the case holds broader lessons for tracking the spread of diseases globally.
The only continent to dodge the virus — until now
Now let's time jump to Australia a few months ago for another bird disease conundrum.

In June, H5N1 — high pathogenicity avian influenza also known as bird flu — arrived in mainland Australia. Up until that point, Australia had been the only continent to dodge the virus which has traversed the globe, leaving a trail of carcasses in its path.

Since late 2021, the virus has led to the death of nearly 300 million poultry birds. Either the virus killed them or they were culled as a preventive measure to stop the spread of the disease, according to the World Animal Health Information System. Further, bird flu is estimated to have killed millions of wild animals and marine mammals, although it's hard to get an exact figure.
Researchers were amazed that Australia could stay bird-flu-free for six years. And the virus didn't take the path that scientists expected.

"We have a lot of migration of birds between Australia and Southeast Asia, so for the first few years, we're like: That's where the virus is coming from," says Dr. Amandine Gamble, an assistant professor at Cornell University in the Department of Public and Ecosystem Health.
The way bird flu eventually got there was from the other direction. It came from Antarctica likely via migrating birds.

"This is a virus that's not assisted by airplanes," Michelle Wille, senior research fellow at the Center for Pathogen Genomics at the University of Melbourne, told NPR in 2025. "This is a virus that's traveling by mass mortality after mass mortality after mass mortality after mass mortality."
"The virus loads are low"
So when Vanstreels set sail to check on the penguins, he assumed bird flu would be the culprit.
Bird flu arrived in Antarctica in late 2023 and early 2024. Vanstreels and his colleagues rapidly arranged for a trip to try to figure out exactly what was happening.

"The expedition was initially fully set up to look for bird flu because that was the panic," he explains, adding that ongoing fear of a continuing global panzootic — or pandemic among animals — is justified.
In several layers of warm clothes covered by protective gear — double gloves, coveralls, glasses and masks — Vanstreels and the team started taking samples of the penguin corpses they found.
"We looked a little bit stiff when walking — like a penguin walking almost — because of all the gear," he says. "We had very strict biosafety standards."
They brought samples from the deceased penguins back to a mini-lab on their boat. By evening, they had early results. But not the results they expected.
"There is bird flu here, but the virus loads are low," he recalls. "That was a little bit puzzling."

The carcasses were not very old, so Vanstreels would have expected to find far more bird flu virus if that had killed the birds. Perhaps something else was the main driver? "We were unsure what was happening," he recalls.
What the microscope revealed
So what killed the 500-plus penguins on the landing ramp and the many others on the island?

Back on land several months after the voyage, in the Netherlands, Vanstreels' colleagues did more investigation. "Under the microscope, you can see that there's bacteria in the tissues," he says — not virus.
They discovered a different disease, a bacterial disease that causes avian cholera (which is distinct from human cholera).
Vanstreels and his team's findings were published in October in the journal the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
So how worried are they about avian cholera?

The disease is not considered a major threat to humans since the strain that is specialized to birds is distinct from the strain specialized to mammals. "The risk for human infection is not really that high when you see an outbreak on birds," Vanstreels says. But, it does kill birds worldwide — especially in cold environments where the bacteria thrives.

While there's not enough research to know exactly how common avian cholera is, the disease has been on the radar of scientists for decades. However, it's not exactly top of mind. The last time researchers looked for it in the Antarctic Peninsula was 25 years ago.

"One could be misled to think that: Well, that was a unique thing that happened back in 2001, and nothing's happened ever since," says Vanstreels. Instead, it is possible that avian cholera die-offs could be occurring regularly, only scientists haven't been checking.
One of his big takeaways from this bird-flu-that-turned-out-to-be-avian-cholera event?
"Yes, there is a big thing with bird flu. But we still want to keep checking for the other diseases because they might be mixing up in the middle," Vanstreels says.
Antarctica isn't as remote as it seems
Like any good mystery, the case of the cholera-stricken penguins has got scientists wondering: Whodunit?
There's a theory that avian cholera might have been introduced to Antarctica decades ago from researchers who brought poultry from the U.S., Vanstreels says.

Gamble, of Cornell University, adds that the strain of avian cholera found in penguins in Antarctica is "very close" to the strain found 5,000 miles away on Île Amsterdam in the Southern Indian Ocean.
"Antarctica is way more connected to the rest of the world than we think it is," she says.
It's hard to track diseases in Antarctica but, she says, it's turning out to be an important piece in the global pathogen puzzle.

The work of keeping tabs on what's happening has fallen to a number of different countries since Antarctica is not governed by any one government. It was designated as a continent of peace and science by the mid 20th-century Antarctic Treaty, which now has 58 parties — among them are the U.S., France, Japan and Russia. Many nations have research stations and team up on scientific undertakings, including tracking pathogens — be it bird flu or avian cholera — that travel great distances and don't respect borders.
"So this Avian cholera outbreak is just showing this is not a unique event," says Gamble. "We really need international collaboration."

articles.headline: Democrats have big healthcare plans. The industry is preparing for a fight.
keyFacts: According to campaign reports, healthcare corporations are backing Republicans and lobbying Democrats to counter progressive healthcare proposals.
Industry groups argue that sweeping policy changes like a public option would reduce access and stifle competition.
Experts say the next two years will determine whether health companies can convince Democrats to scale back policy ambitions.
body: Americans want changes to their healthcare, and the candidates in this year’s midterms are making bold promises about how they are going to improve it: Medicare-for-all, or a public health insurance option, or free primary care for everyone. If Democrats win big this year, they could build up momentum to control Congress and the White House in 2029, which could leave them well-positioned to take on the thorny problem of how to fix the US health system.
Democrats have big healthcare plans. The industry is preparing for a fight.
Corporations have always fought universal healthcare proposals. But will their old playbook still work in a new era?

History suggests that this won’t be easy. For every Affordable Care Act, you have the failed attempt to repeal it or the calamity of the Clinton-era healthcare initiative. Americans want change — but they fear it, too. I’ve spent years reading healthcare polls, talking to voters, attending focus groups. The public’s opinion of the healthcare industry has grown more and more sour, and distrust of the medical establishment is at an all-time high. People are sick of having a broken health system, but they worry that big changes could end up being bad for them.
Even though a meaningful attempt at reform is still years away and universal health care in any form might seem like a progressive pipe dream, the industry is not sitting idly by.

As Democrats have started to roll out policy proposals in anticipation of winning back Congress, the industry has been there to start making its case. In some campaigns, that means backing Republicans, but it also means lobbying Democratic Party leaders to hold the line against their more progressive members who want to push for far-reaching changes.
The question now is: Will their old playbook work? Can the industry convince Democrats to scale back their policy ambitions, or is their grip on Congress loosening?

“The next two years are actually quite pivotal, for doing the groundwork and all the necessary socializing, consensus-building,” said Kim Monk, a former congressional healthcare staffer who co-founded the private-sector research firm Capital Alpha Partners. “That’s the work that gets you to a point where either party decides, okay, this will be on our platform — or not.”

That will be the tug-of-war of the next two years: a PR battle waged between health companies with hundreds of millions of dollars at their disposal on one side and progressive lawmakers, activists, and patient advocates on the other that will ultimately determine what’s possible in the next phase of American healthcare.
The healthcare industry doesn’t want Democrats to win too big
In the short term, the industry is hedging its bets in the face of a Democratic wave.

Private enterprise has historically backed the Republican Party, but that’s starting to shift. What the healthcare industry values above all else is balance. Democrats operating without any constraints are more likely to impose government regulations on medical companies. But full GOP control comes with its own risks, like the $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts passed as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which has already led to clinics and hospitals laying off staff or even closing facilities altogether.

Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy. Sign up here.

“At least for the short term, I imagine the healthcare industry would welcome control of Congress by Democrats, creating more predictability, forestalling more cuts in Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act, and potentially reversing or delaying some of the cuts that have already been made,” said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF. “The longer-term political calculus for the healthcare industry is more complicated. Many Democrats are pushing for a bigger role for government in health care.”

In other words, while healthcare companies might welcome a Democratic House as a check on President Donald Trump’s unpredictability, they aren’t necessarily hoping for a massive blue wave that could make significant reforms a serious possibility if Democrats were to win the White House in 2028.

The industry’s MO when it looks like a wave election is brewing is to balance the scales: I reported in 2016 how, in what was looking like a good year for Democrats, the drug industry poured money into the campaigns of Republican candidates by a 6-to-1 margin in competitive races, hoping to stifle the agenda of presumed President Hillary Clinton. (Of course they, like the rest of us, are still susceptible to being wrong.)
And that’s how the industry has been approaching the 2026 election: In many of the pivotal House and Senate races, they are backing the GOP.

As healthcare journalist Merrill Goozner reported last week, the American Hospital Association PAC and PhRMA, a drug industry trade group, have given a combined $14,500 to Republican incumbent Jon Husted and none to his Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown in the historically expensive Ohio Senate race. In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins has received donations from all of the major healthcare trade groups — hospitals, pharma, insurers, and doctors — while her opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, got none. (He also has sworn off corporate PAC money.) Even in an open race without an incumbent, like the Iowa Senate campaign, the Republican candidate has scored donations from hospitals and pharma, but the Democrat has not, Goozner reported.

If Democrats take the House but not the Senate, that would immediately put a damper on their healthcare reform plans — whereas winning a Senate majority would allow them to start drafting and debating bills in both chambers with an eye toward what could actually pass if they win in 2028 too.

“If there is actually a blue tsunami next week and Democrats get 51-plus [members] in the Senate, that’s a really big deal,” Monk said. “You can’t just say this doesn’t matter because Trump’s going to veto it, because I think it very much becomes a 2028 issue.”
And even as they work to push the next Congress more to their ideological liking, the healthcare industry is preparing for the fight that comes after.
The industry is prepping its counterattacks on ambitious healthcare proposals

After the midterms wrap up, the next two years in Congress and on the presidential campaign trail will be crucial. The industry is already working to set the terms of the debate and push back against big changes.

Each subset of the industry has its own versions of this argument: Pharma warns that price controls could stifle innovation, insurers warn that coverage mandates will increase premiums, hospitals warn that constraints on their funding could lead to closures and job losses. (There’s a well-known saying among DC insiders that every congressional district has a hospital, making every member potentially susceptible to the industry’s message that new healthcare legislation could result in their own constituents losing their jobs.)

They’ve started by trying to discredit the more sweeping health policy proposals before new members ever arrive in Washington, DC. In Texas, for instance, Republican groups have leaned on an industry-commissioned study to attack Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico for supporting Medicare-for-all, warning that it would lead to cuts for rural hospitals — at least according to an analysis produced by the Partnership for America’s Future, a coalition of industry groups that exists explicitly to oppose Medicare-for-all or a public option. They ran a similar ad against Democrat Janelle Stelson, who’s trying to topple incumbent Rep. Scott Perry in Pennsylvania.

The industry is trying to plant the idea in voters’ minds that these big, bold proposals may sound superficially appealing, but carry significant risks: You could lose your plan, you could lose your doctor, you could pay higher taxes. (And they often have their own studies to back those arguments, like the one cited in this year’s campaign, to counter the evidence offered by advocates in support of reform.) And it might work exactly like it has in the past. As John McDonough, a former congressional healthcare staffer and author of America’s Wrong Turn: US Health Care in the Neoliberal Era, put it to me, the history is clear: “Every comprehensive effort, defeat, and every incremental effort succeeds.” That is in part because of the healthcare industry’s influence and its success in framing the debate.

On top of trying to sway the competitive races, the industry is also trying to keep its most important allies within both parties happy ahead of the midterms. As the Center for Health and Democracy’s data shows, the health insurance industry PACs alone have given tens of thousands of dollars to Democratic and Republican leaders, as well as senior members of the healthcare-focused House and Senate committees.

It’s another hedge, an attempt to keep the members who will decide what’s on the agenda next year on their side. The industry supports reversing the GOP’s massive Medicaid cuts and increasing funding for the ACA marketplaces, two top-priority items for Democrats if they win Congress in the midterms. But they are hoping the party’s leaders will steer their members away from some of their more radical ideas for overhauling healthcare. Because while individual sectors within healthcare may squabble over smaller-scale reforms, the entire industry is united against plans to fundamentally change the US health system. (They are also increasingly owned by the same parent company, as consolidation in the medical sector becomes more and more common.)
“The healthcare industry is all for more people having coverage and stable government financing,” Levitt said, “but will circle the wagons to fight Medicare-for-all.”

Already, whenever Democrats start talking about their health policy ideas, the industry is ready with a response. Last month, as some Democrats announced support for a public insurance option, the Partnership for America’s Health Care Future argued it would reduce access. “A public option is not the answer to the affordability and access challenges patients and families are facing,” said the group’s executive director, Lauren Crawford Shaver.

Meanwhile, the health insurance lobbying group, AHIP, released a 40-page document in October on how to improve affordability and access, using it in part to argue against a public option because it would “stifle competition and threaten the coverage most Americans want to keep.” Centrist Democratic groups who receive industry support have said they are “preparing for war” against Medicare-for-all, according to the news outlet Sludge.

The industry is not omnipotent, however, and the debate could still change if Americans’ healthcare gets worse over the next few years. The US uninsured rate has been on the rise as pandemic protections expire and the costs of healthcare rise for millions. Unless Democrats succeed in stopping the Republican Medicaid and ACA cuts in the OBBBA, that problem is going to get worse — and that could also force Democrats to think bigger about how to fix it.

“I am not sure anyone has fully absorbed how damaging and disruptive that is going to be — including to hospitals and health systems,” Jonathan Oberlander, professor of social medicine at the University of North Carolina and the former editor of the Journal of Health Politics, Policy and Law, told me over email. “Large coverage losses will trigger great instability in health politics and perhaps open more of a window to bolder proposals.”

So, will the industry’s arguments still have juice? After the medical industry enjoyed a brief rebound in popularity during the pandemic, 50 percent of Americans say they have a negative view of it, while 37 percent have a positive view, per Gallup. And the appetite for reform is growing: 64 percent of Americans say it is the government’s responsibility to make sure that everyone has healthcare coverage — the highest share at any time, except for the late 2000s, shortly before the ACA became law.

Even the hospital industry, which has long enjoyed more public support than pharma or insurance companies, is seeing its popularity waver: A Families USA poll from August found that an overwhelming 81 percent of Americans thought hospital prices were unreasonable.

“Hospitals have done a great job of pleading poverty on Capitol Hill. ‘We’re probably the only provider who basically has to provide care to whoever shows up. We have no reason to be efficient. Just give us more money,’” Monk said. “I think that argument is wearing a little bit thin.”

articles.headline: Patrick Stewart, actor known for iconic roles in ‘Star Trek’ and ‘X-Men,’ dies at 86
keyFacts: Actor Patrick Stewart has died at age 86 following an Alzheimer’s and Lewy body dementia diagnosis, his spokesperson confirmed.
Stewart was famous for playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film series.
Marvel Studios and co-star Hugh Jackman were among those who paid tribute to Stewart following his passing.
body: Beloved actor Patrick Stewart has died following a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, his representative confirmed. He was 86.

“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” Kelly Bush Novak, his longtime spokesperson, said in a statement provided to NBC News on Thursday.

Stewart — whose storied career included the iconic roles of Professor X in the “X-Men” film series and Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in the “Star Trek” franchise — had spent quality time with loved ones before his death, according to the statement.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” the statement said. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection of his invincible grace.”

An indelible part of the “Star Trek” legacy, he played Jean-Luc Picard for seven seasons on “Star Trek: The Next Generation” from 1987 to 1994 and in multiple films, and reprised the role in the Paramount+ show “Star Trek: Picard,” from 2020 to 2023.
He stepped into the role of Professor Charles Xavier with the 2000 film “X-Men,” and continued to depict the genius mutant telepath in multiple sequels.
He was featured in a trailer for the highly anticipated “Avengers: Doomsday” film scheduled to be released in December, reprising the role for the eighth time in the mega Marvel crossover.
He had most recently done voice over work in the film “The Sheep Detectives” and appeared in the Prime Video series “Bait,” both in 2026, according to his IMDb profile.

Born in the town of Mirfield in West Yorkshire, England, he joined the acclaimed Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966. He went on to make his Broadway debut in 1971 in “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” and forged a career on the silver screen.

“His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre,” the statement said. “He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise.”
Off the stage, he was dedicated to philanthropy and activism, including advocating for human rights, domestic violence survivors, refugees, veteran mental health services and animal welfare.

A revered figure in Hollywood — with myriad accolades spanning nominations for Emmy Awards, Golden Globes and Screen Actors Guild Awards — he was also knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his services to drama.

The statement closed with a quote from his 2023 book, “Making It So: A Memoir,” that said: “Like me, Jean-Luc has lived an unusual life that has taken him far beyond the bounds of normal human experience. But he is also someone who has remained true to his earthbound roots, for they are what gave him his identity. In the end, he feels the call of home, as do I.”
Marvel Studios said in a statement it is “deeply saddened” by Stewart’s passing.

“Sir Patrick brought Professor Charles Xavier to life with extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from ‘X-Men’ to ‘Logan’ to ‘Avengers: Doomsday,’” the statement said. “He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman. Our hearts go out to his wife Sunny, his children, his friends, and the countless fans around the world whose lives he touched with his art.”
Kevin Feige, President of Marvel Studios, recalled first seeing Stewart in action.

“I’ll never forget the first time I saw Sir Patrick Stewart on the set of the first X-Men. After years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe — and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas,” Feige said in a statement to NBC News.

“Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor. It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed,” he added.
Tributes poured in for Stewart from devoted fans and co-stars.

Hugh Jackman, who played Wolverine to Stewart’s Professor X in the “X-Men” films, shared photos of the pair on Instagram, writing: “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”

articles.headline: Topcoat enables Rust to render server-side web apps
keyFacts: Amazon Web Services engineer Carl Lerche demonstrated Topcoat, a new framework for running server-side web applications written in Rust.
Topcoat compiles Rust code into JavaScript and executes logic on the server to reduce loading times for typical database-driven web applications.
Frontend developer Ken Kohlman said Topcoat offers impressive simplicity, though he noted it is best suited for smaller web projects.
body: Popular for other uses, Rust isn't typically deployed for web development. That could change, however.

With AI here to do the heavy lifting, coders may want to consider the programming language, given its runtime performance and safety guarantees, suggested Carl Lerche , an Amazon Web Services principal engineer, speaking at ScyllaDB’s 2026 P99 virtual conference last week.
Lerche was there to demonstrate his latest project, Topcoat , a framework for running web applications written in Rust.
Lerche is perhaps best known for creating Tokio , which is the most popular asynchronous Rust runtime in that ecosystem.
“Three years ago, had [I] gone out and said that Rust could be the best language for building web apps, you probably would have called me crazy,” he told the virtual audience.
Web developers gravitate towards the languages they find most familiar. These days, that means JavaScript, or possibly Ruby.

A number of web frameworks already use Rust. Both Leptos and Dioxus compile Rust into WebAssembly, which most browsers run. This approach is great for heavy computational jobs, though the upfront loading time can be a real drag.
Topcoat compiles your Rust code into more web-friendly JavaScript. For Lerche, JavaScript remains the best way to interact with the browser's Document Object Model (DOM).

“Generally, the approach taken by any Rust framework can be traced back to another ecosystem, usually a very popular one. You can't really point to a single existing framework as [Topcoat’s] main source of inspiration,” noted frontend developer Ken Kohlman, in a summary video on his “Code to the Moon” YouTube channel.
Walk on the server side

Lerche admitted that Topcoat isn’t for building complex applications, on the scale of, say, Figma, but it can easily be used for the run-of-the-mill, browser-based, database-driven applications, which is to say 90 percent of the web today.

Unlike most present-day JavaScript frameworks , Topcoat eschews the current definition of being reactive, where the program logic is dumped onto the browser when the session begins. Instead, most of the logic executes on the server, with only the results delivered to the browser (Developers can still write client-side logic using a subset of Rust, which Topcoat automatically compiles into JavaScript for the browser).

It’s an old idea recast with better tech. Server-side rendering predates reactive programming (see Apache’s server-side includes ). With server-side rendering, Lerche admitted, “It might sound like we're going back to the old days of full page refreshes for every click [but] you can actually get almost all of what you think of as reactive with server-side rendering.”

But server-side programming has been making a comeback lately, especially for those devs disgruntled with React and other frameworks. HTMX , Datastar , and Phoenix LiveView all render web pages on the server, sending them back to the browser nearly completed.

Topcoat is just tweaking their ideas to fit well with Rust, Lerche said. When a user smashes a button on a web page, the whole page isn’t refreshed. Just the HTML snippet for that component is returned and refreshed by the server.
JavaScript in the front, Rust in the back

Topcoat saves load times by rendering all the components at once, rather than one by one. Also, data loading does not block the loading of the page. The server can send back a web page with placeholders into which the data will stream.

One big dollop of secret sauce that Topcoat has is that it provides a way for the component, which is already on the server, to speak directly to the database, thanks to an earlier project from Lerche called Toasty , a Rust-based asynchronous database object-relational mapper (which he spoke about at P99 2024).
“You can do your rendering right with the data immediately, so you don't have to figure out how to serialize it, send it to the client, deserialize it,” he said.

By pushing data loading deep down into the page render, the server can send the head of the HTML template to the client immediately, allowing the browser to start preloading assets (like CSS or images) while the server renders the rest of the page.

“The simplicity is incredible, and it is something that we have been sorely missing in this space. I feel like someone who doesn't really know Rust could get off the ground pretty quickly with this thing,” Kohlman said. He did agree with Lerche that Topcoat is best for smaller web projects, given that Topcoat only uses a subset of the Rust syntax.
“There's something to be said for having the full Rust syntax at your disposal,” he said. ®

articles.headline: Frank Miller Teases Sin City Future and Finally Drawing Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles
keyFacts: Frank Miller announced that his upcoming Wild West prequel comic, Sin City: Blood & Dust, is about two-thirds drawn and well along.
Miller discussed his new sci-fi comic Invasive Species, which was inspired by the COVID-19 pandemic and 1950s alien invasion movies.
Miller recently contributed an official cover for Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles #300 after being asked by IDW.
body: Frank Miller is in one of the most prolific periods of his long comics career right now. The creator of iconic stories like The Dark Knight Returns and 300 is spinning up new projects and revisiting classic franchises, all while maintaining his own publishing company, Frank Miller Presents.

We were lucky enough to attend a roundtable interview at the Lucca Comics & Games Festival in Italy, where Miller reflected on his career and the current state of the industry, while also giving some updates on upcoming projects like Sin City: Blood & Dust and Invasive Species. Read on to see the highlights from that fascinating conversation.
The Status of Sin City: Blood & Dust

Miller released a number of Sin City comics in the '90s and early '00s. But even with the Sin City movies drawing wider attention to the franchise, it's been quite some time since Miller has told any new stories in this seedy, noir-infused universe.

That's finally going to change soon. Miller has spent the past several years working on a new book first announced as Sin City 1858 and now called Sin City: Blood & Dust. As the title suggests, Blood & Dust is a prequel set in the Wild West era and detailing the original founding of Basin City. It's a massive undertaking for Miller, as unlike many of his current projects, he's writing and drawing the entire thing himself. But it's one that seems to be coming along nicely.

"I'm not sure exactly when the release date is planned for right now, but the project is very well along," Miller said. "I mean, I'm most of the way through it, and it's certainly all planned and plotted very carefully. And I've drawn, I'd say, about two-thirds of it. And so everything else should flow pretty quickly."

When asked how he's feeling about the project so far, Miller said, "Very good. Very good. It's certainly a departure. If you're going to take a break from a series for a long time, you might as well come back with a very different one."
Teasing Invasive Species

Sin City: Blood & Dust is just one of several projects Miller is currently developing. He was asked if there were any particular books in the works he was especially excited to show to readers. Miller singled out Invasive Species, a new Dark Horse Comcis project that was announced at SDCC 2026 this past summer.

Invasive Species is a sci-fi comic that pairs Miller with artist Ryan Benjamin and colorist Alex Sinclair. Details about the book's plot were scarce before now, but Miller shed more light on it during the panel, revealing it to be a microscopic invasion story inspired by the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Invasive Species is what I'm particularly charged up about," Miller said. "It's a project I conceived during the height of the COVID pandemic where everyone was afraid to sneeze within a hundred yards of anybody else because everybody was so afraid and everyone was wearing masks. I think people were showering their masks. It was so paranoid. But what it reminded me of was those wonderful 1950s alien movies like Invasion of the Body Snatchers and Invaders From Mars and so on. They were all fear of a Russian invasion."

Miller continued, "But I thought we had biological warfare talk everywhere every which way now we've got viruses that we're all afraid of and as guys all locked inside not talking to each other. And I thought what perfect metaphor for our times. And so I made up a story where we were being invaded not by a bunch of spaceships, but by a virus, by little aliens that got inside, came in our ears."
Drawing TMNT

One of the more interesting developments in the comic book world this year came when Miller was among numerous artists tapped to draw a cover for Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles #300. Miller is famously credited as a huge source of inspiration behind Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird's original TMNT comics, so it was a fun case of life imitating art.
We asked Miller for his thoughts on finally contributing to the TMNT franchise in an official capacity. He revealed that IDW didn't exactly have to twist his arm to get him on board.

"There's no agenda to all this stuff," Miller said. "They were kids when they were doing it in their clunky black-and-white comic. No one dreamed they would turn out to have this amazing property, which I think one of the main things they had was one of the best titles in history. So when they asked, I said, 'Sure.' I mean, they were big fans of mine and I thought that this will be fun. And then I sat down and said, 'What do I do with these guys?' I said, 'Well, look, stack them up.' I did it and they were real happy."

As for which Turtle is Miller's favorite, the artist replied, "Well, I have a favorite Renaissance painter. I say Michelangelo because the Sistine Ceiling is one of the best comic book pages I've ever seen."
Will Frank Miller Direct Again?

Miller was able to make the leap from creating comics to directing films thanks to 2005's Sin City. Miller directed a segment of the film in collaboration with Robert Rodriguez and later did the same for the 2014 sequel. The Sin City movie paved the way for Miller to fully direct 2008's The Spirit, based on the classic Will Eisner hero.

The Spirit wasn't exactly well-received, critically or commercially, but it certainly brought a unique visual flourish to the property. We asked Miller if he had any desire to return behind the camera and direct another film at some point.
"Sure. Yeah. I mean, come on," Miller said. "It's an amazing field. It's an amazing form and it's like nothing else in the world."
Miller added, "I mean, that's like asking a kid if he wants to fly the Millennium Falcon."
For more, learn about the major revelations in Absolute Batman #25 and see an exclusive preview of The Infernal Hulk vs. The Avengers .

articles.headline: Your headphones have hidden LE Audio features you’ll want to know about
keyFacts: LE Audio improves wireless device performance by consolidating profiles for simultaneous high-quality voice calls and audio streaming.
Native multi-stream audio in LE Audio sends independent streams to each earbud, preventing asymmetrical battery drain.
LE Audio eliminates proprietary codec fragmentation issues to deliver lower latency and improved audio streams on compatible devices.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- LE Audio is more than Auracast.
- Bluetooth headphones with LE Audio transmit audio in new ways across the board.
- Your LE Audio headphones have several less-discussed new tricks.

The shift from Classic Bluetooth to LE Audio is in full swing, as JBL and Sony release flagship headphones and earbuds with built-in LE Audio. Bose is the latest to upgrade its flagship headphones via an OTA firmware update.
Better voice quality

LE Audio includes the Low Complexity Communication Codec (LC3), which includes the unified Telephony and Media Audio Profile (TMAP) to handle audio streams and voice calls simultaneously. Bluetooth Classic relies on the Advanced Audio Distribution Profile (A2DP) and Hands-Free Profile (HFP), which handle the same functions but require both profiles.

The profiles in Bluetooth Classic, given that they must alternate, result in extremely poor voice quality during hands-free calls over cellular or video calls on Zoom or Teams. These profiles also account for degraded voice quality when chatting while playing a mobile game.
LE Audio consolidates these two profiles, creating higher-quality, bidirectional audio and preserving voice call quality when using wireless headphones.
Battery drain no more

Earlier this year, JBL gave its flagship Tour Pro 3 earbuds an OTA firmware update to support LE Audio, and Sony’s WF-1000XM6 earbuds, released in February, have LE Audio support out of the box. There’s one major true wireless earbud improvement wrapped in LE Audio: native multi-stream audio.

In Bluetooth Classic, your source device, such as your phone, sends audio to one earbud, which then retransmits it to the other earbud. This complex audio transmission method is why one of your earbuds always has a lower battery than the other. Though premium earbuds usually have an independent stream workaround, many midrange and budget earbuds don’t, and that’s where LE Audio comes in handy.
LE Audio enables independent audio streams built into the Bluetooth stack, so manufacturers don’t need to implement their own methods to avoid asymmetrical battery drain.
Breaking down ecosystems

Software ecosystems, like Apple’s iOS and Samsung’s Galaxy, dictate which audio features are reserved for devices inside of them and withhold features from devices outside of them. Hardware ecosystems are equally responsible for the fragmentation of audio features across manufacturers, typically through codecs.

Sony’s LDAC codec for high-quality audio is only available on Sony headphones, earbuds, and smartphones with the proper hardware, which is limited in the US market. Snapdragon’s AptX codecs aren’t as widely available on phones either, leaving most people to rely on Bluetooth Classic SBC and AAC codes, even though their headphones support more advanced ones.
LE Audio eliminates the tedious codec issue, especially in wireless gaming contexts, delivering lower latency, improved voice audio streams, and eliminating asymmetrical audio transmission.

For now, as long as you have a compatible Android phone, you have access to several models of headphones, earbuds, and Bluetooth speakers that support LE Audio. As more manufacturers update their devices to support the Bluetooth audio streaming protocol, this suggests the technology is becoming more reliable.
So, what about your AirPods? I wouldn’t bet on it anytime soon.
